chapter_theme: Neelakesi, leaving Kapilapuram after defeating the Buddha, sings a hymn claiming that all faultless scripture and every true god belong to the Jina and that he knows without reckoning; she reaches the Ajivikas at Samadandam, where Puranan names Makkali as their silent omniscient Lord, the nine Kathir books as scripture, and five categories of atom (earth, water, fire, wind and soul) that never enter one another; she undertakes to show this contrary to perception and reason, and begins by arguing that a Lord who never spoke left no scripture and that silence cannot make a Lord.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the most learned of the Ajivika ascetics at Samadandam, their spokesman in the debate
the Ajivika ascetics gathered in the grove at Samadandam

659.reading: Leaving Kapilapuram behind, Neelakesi travels by the sky path, vast as a mountain, and begins to praise the one of shining body who shed the inner four deeds and knows without having to reckon.
659.nuance: எண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான், 'he who knew without reckoning', is the mark she earlier denied the Buddha, who she said knew by seeing, hearing and reckoning (193). உண்ணால் வினை is read as உள் நால் வினை, the four inner deeds, which fits the Jain account of the omniscient but is a reading of a joined form.
659.event: Neelakesi leaves Kapilapuram by the sky and begins a hymn to the Jina.

claims.claim: the Lord, rid of the inner deeds, knows all things without reasoning his way to them

660.reading: She asks whether any word of the other schools free of fault lies outside the ocean of scripture told by the one who gave the Angas, any more than there is a flower that does not come to rest at the Lord's red feet.
660.nuance: The verse turns on a rhetorical question whose force can be read two ways: that no rival school speaks without fault, or that whatever is faultless in them is already in the Jina's scripture; the parallel with the flowers that all end at the Lord's feet favours the second.

claims.claim: whatever is faultless in the other schools' words is already contained in the Jina's scripture

661.reading: She asks whether there is any penance-path that ends birth not found in the scripture-ocean of the one who gave the Purvas, and likewise whether there is any god who does not bear the Tirthankara's holy name.
661.nuance: The second half folds every god of every school into the Jina: whatever is rightly worshipped as a god is a name of the Tirthankara.

claims.claim: every path of penance that ends birth is taught in the scripture of the Purvas
every true god is a name of the Tirthankara

662.reading: She asks where there is any scripture the world recites that does not draw on the learning the Poet uttered, and says that the world's scriptures and much else besides were born of what he said.

claims.claim: the scriptures other peoples recite are derived from the Jina's teaching

663.reading: Adorned with flowers and sandal, she says she knows nothing but her Lord's flower feet, and asks that those feet bring her, who knows nothing else, through to the end.

664.reading: She has no joy except in the paired feet of the Lord who was first in the world, and trusts those feet to bring her, who has no other joy, to birth in the state where suffering is put away.

claims.claim: devotion to the Jina's feet brings one to the state where suffering is removed

665.reading: Nothing is in her mind but the holy feet of the one who knows without approaching, like a fine gem shining in the night, and she trusts those feet to give her, whose mind holds nothing else, great power.
665.nuance: அண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான, 'who knew without coming near', repeats the claim of 659 that the Lord's knowing does not go through the senses' contact with things.

666.reading: Praying that the old deeds gathered on her may end, she worships the feet of the Lord of the triple umbrella in thought, word and body, and from the great city of Kukkuta goes like a flag of lightning into Samadandam.
666.nuance: The convert who once begged the sage to quench her cruel deeds (62) now asks the Jina's feet for the same thing; the prayer is hers, and the verse does not say how the feet are to end the deeds.
666.event: Neelakesi worships the Jina's feet, praying to be rid of her old deeds, and goes from Kukkuta city to Samadandam.

667.reading: To the ascetics gathered there she says that the grove of fragrant flowers is lovely to see and asks who these are that dwell in it.
667.event: Neelakesi comes on the Ajivika ascetics in their flowering grove and asks who they are.

668.reading: From that throng of godlike ones who want no cause, Puranan, greatly learned and greatest of them, speaks so that the woman may know.
668.nuance: காரணம் வேண்டாக் கடவுட் குழாம், 'the god-throng that needs no cause', may be a Jain's barb at the Ajivika teaching that things come about without cause; the phrase can also be plain praise of ascetics who want nothing.
668.event: Puranan, the most learned of the Ajivikas, steps forward to answer her.

669.reading: Puranan tells her that these are not strangers but Ajivikas, great ascetics of undeluded vision at whom all the wide world marvels.
669.event: Puranan names his company as the Ajivikas.

670.reading: Neelakesi, unequalled in every science, tells him that much is gained by setting out in order the teacher, the scripture, the categories and how they come about, and asks him to state his scripture here.
670.nuance: Her four heads (ஆத்தன், நூல், பொருள், நிகழ்ச்சி) are the questions the king of Kampili put at the first debate (172), now in her own mouth: she has become the examiner.
670.event: Neelakesi asks Puranan to set out his teacher, scripture, categories and their workings.

671.reading: Puranan answers that Makkali himself is the Lord, that their scripture is the nine books called Kathir, that the subtle categories are five, and that their working is fixedness (காழ்ப்பாடு).
671.nuance: Neelakesi answers each head in turn: the authority of the books in 680-681, the five categories in 687-693, and the காழ்ப்பாடு in 694, where she calls it a fixity of bewilderment. காழ்ப்பாடு, 'hardening', is read as the fixed course of things; the word is rare and its exact sense is not secure.
671.event: Puranan names Makkali as the Ajivikas' god and states their scripture and categories.

claims.claim: Makkali is the Lord
the Ajivika scripture is the nine books called Kathir
the subtle categories are five
the working of the categories is fixed

672.reading: Puranan says the Lord is Lord because he knew, and kept himself closed; were he to speak without restraint, he would be like one who has thrown something and would fall back, bewildered, into the round of wandering.
672.nuance: This is the Ajivika ground for a silent omniscient: to speak is to be moved, and to be moved is to fall back into birth. Neelakesi takes the verse up almost word for word in 682 to answer it. The simile எறிந்தான் அனைய (like one who threw) is compressed and its exact point is not certain.

claims.claim: the omniscient Lord stays silent, since speaking would draw him back into the round of births

673.reading: Puranan describes the Lord as one who neither speaks nor eats, has no wrinkle or grey hair, and has a form that cannot be seen, like a rainbow in the sky that no bound contains.
673.nuance: The last words, புகழ் பூரணனே, may close the speech with the speaker's name or may call the Lord the Full One (பூரணன்); the division of line 4 allows either. Neelakesi turns the rainbow simile against him in 684.

claims.claim: the Lord neither speaks nor eats nor ages, and his form is unseen like a rainbow

674.reading: Puranan says the matters spoken of in the Kathir, beginning with restraint and the goal, when gathered come to this: there are atoms, and they are of five forms.
674.nuance: உணு in line 4 is read as அணு.

claims.claim: all that the scripture treats comes down to atoms of five kinds

675.reading: Puranan names the five as earth, water, fire, wind and soul, each with its many qualities, and says that, sound apart, coolness is the first quality of water.
675.nuance: Soul counted as the fifth beside the four elements is the same five the Manimekalai's Ajivika gives. Line 3 is hard to divide, and which quality is assigned to earth is not clear.

claims.claim: the five categories are earth, water, fire, wind and soul, each with its own qualities

676.reading: Puranan says burning and the like belong to fire, compacting and feeding to wind, turning back and knowing to soul, and that these are the qualities of the substances named.
676.nuance: Knowing is listed as one quality among the others, the soul's as burning is fire's; Neelakesi's attack on the five classes begins at 687.

claims.claim: knowing is the quality proper to soul, as burning is to fire

677.reading: Puranan says the five kinds of atom all combine and separate, but that one does not enter into another, not even for an instant.
677.nuance: Neelakesi answers this in 698, where she presses him that, if nothing gives room to anything else, ghee cannot become flame. Line 2's குணமே இலவாம் seems to deny the atoms qualities just after 676 gave them; the reading is unsure.

claims.claim: atoms combine and part but never enter one another

678.reading: Puranan says these are the categories and he will tell something of their nature for the assembly, warns her not to scorn the Ajivikas as caring only for taste, and claims the categories cannot be overthrown by others.

claims.claim: the Ajivika categories cannot be overthrown by rival schools

679.reading: When he has named the Lord, scripture, categories and their working, Neelakesi, of skilled speech, sets out before the learned company to show that all of it is contrary both to sight and to reason, and speaks again.
679.nuance: கண்ணினும் அன்றிக் கருத்தினும் வேறு: she will test his account by perception and by inference, the two means both sides grant, not by her own scripture.
679.event: Neelakesi begins her answer, undertaking to show the Ajivika account contrary to perception and reason.

680.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the one who knew everything kept silence and never spoke, then the books were spoken by souls full of hatred and other faults, so they are not scripture, and she asks him, fool, how he came by them.

claims.claim: if the omniscient never spoke, the books in his name are the words of passion-bound souls and have no authority

681.reading: She goes on that if he says the two gods Okkali and Yokali told the books, then had they known as Makkali knew they too would have kept silent, and to speak of the truth without knowing it is unfit, so what these teachers said is faulty.
681.nuance: Okkali and Yokali are otherwise unknown in the corpus; the verse treats them as the Ajivika's fallback authors. இக்கலியாளர் may pun on Makkali's name and on கலி, the dark age.

claims.claim: one who speaks of the truth without knowing it is not a fit authority

682.reading: Taking up his words, she says that if a knower who speaks what he knows becomes subject to longing and anger and falls back into wandering by that fault, then, by his own reasoning, he too would become a lesser Apta by sitting silent.
682.nuance: The verse reuses the words of 672 (அறிந்தான், எறிந்தான் அனைய, மறிந்தான், தடுமாற்று) to turn them: if silence is what makes the Lord, any silent man is one. The last line is compressed and its turn is a reading.

claims.claim: silence alone cannot be what makes one an omniscient Lord

links.note: In the Kundalakesi debate Neelakesi said the Buddha knew only by seeing, hearing and reckoning (எண்ணியும் உணர்தலால்); her hymn now praises the Jina as the one who knew without reckoning (எண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான்).
links.teaches: The epithet in the hymn is a debating point turned into praise: the Jina is defined by exactly the mode of knowing she denied the Buddha, so the hymn carries the earlier argument into worship.

links.note: The king of Kampili asked the debaters for their first teacher, his scripture, its matters and their workings; Neelakesi now puts the same heads (ஆத்தன், நூல், பொருள், நிகழ்ச்சி) to the Ajivika.
links.teaches: The heads that a king imposed on the first debate have become Neelakesi's own method, so the epic shows the convert taking over the judge's role as well as the debater's.

links.note: Manimekalai asks the Jain for his lord, his categories, their workings, and bondage and release; Neelakesi asks the Ajivika for his teacher, scripture, categories and their workings.
links.teaches: Both epics question rival schools by nearly the same heads, but the Jain examiner puts scripture in place of bondage and release, and her first attack (680) falls on the scripture, so the choice of heads already aims the refutation.

links.note: Manimekalai's Ajivika spokesman, Puranan, gives as god a knower without limit present everywhere, and five categories, soul and four atoms; Neelakesi's Puranan gives Makkali as god, the nine Kathir books as scripture, and five categories.
links.teaches: A Buddhist and a Jain polemic agree on the Ajivika spokesman's name and the five categories, which points to the Ajivikas' own teaching, but only the Jain account makes Makkali the god, which sets up its attack on a silent omniscient whose books no one heard.

links.note: Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another (ஒன்று ஒன்றில் புகுதா); Neelakesi's says they combine and part but one does not enter another.
links.teaches: Two hostile accounts state the same tenet in nearly the same words, so it is likely the Ajivikas' own, and the Jain debater singles it out for attack (698) where the Buddhist narrator lets it pass.

links.note: Puranan says the Lord kept silent because speaking would cast him back into wandering; Neelakesi repeats his words and turns them, so that silence would make any silent man a lesser Lord.
links.teaches: The refutation works by repeating the opponent's own verse almost word for word, so the reader sees how a Neelakesi debate argues: the rival's premise is restated and pushed to an absurd consequence.

links.note: The hymn in the Kundalakesi sarukkam says the Lord never says 'I will speak' yet has a voice like a drum, and has no mind to harm; the Ajivika holds that a knower who speaks falls into longing and anger.
links.teaches: The hymn's paradox of a Lord who speaks without willing to speak turns out to be the Jain answer to the Ajivika's dilemma, so a line that reads as devotion is doctrine aimed at this debate.

links.note: Kural 4 sets the Lord apart as one without liking or aversion; Puranan argues that a knower who speaks must fall into longing and anger, and Neelakesi denies that speech implies them.
links.teaches: The Kural defines its Lord by the absence of liking and aversion without asking whether such a Lord can teach; the Ajivika debate shows that the absence was contested, since a rival held that any speaking Lord must have them.

gains.a: the epic's debate gains a well-known Tamil statement of the passionless Lord that Neelakesi's position needs and the Ajivika's denies
gains.b: the couplet gains a live dispute over whether its Lord could speak at all without losing the very freedom from liking and aversion it praises

links.note: Tirumular tells the devotee to take refuge in the shade of the one God's feet so that the sea of deeds will not reach him; Neelakesi, a Jain convert, prays at the Jina's feet that her old deeds may end.
links.teaches: A Jain convert and a Saiva poet both bring their deeds to a Lord's feet in prayer, so the difference between Jain release by wearing deeds away and Saiva release by grace is not visible in the act of worship but only in the doctrine behind it.

gains.a: the epic's prayer gains a Saiva statement of what refuge at the feet is supposed to do, against which the Jain hymn's silence about how the feet end deeds stands out
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a rival tradition that uses the same act of refuge at the feet without his one all-pervading God

links.note: Puranan likens the Lord's unseen form to a rainbow that no bound contains; Neelakesi answers that a rainbow is made when sunlight falls on rain-cloud.
links.teaches: The simile chosen to set Makkali beyond causes is turned into an example of a thing produced by conditions, so the Ajivika's own image testifies against a Lord without cause.

links.note: Neelakesi first argues that a silent omniscient leaves his books without authority; in 685 she adds that if silence proved full knowledge, children, trees and mountains would share it.
links.teaches: The attack on the silent Lord has two steps: silence cuts off the scripture, and silence cannot serve as evidence of knowledge, so the Ajivika is left with neither a speaking teacher nor a proof of his teacher.

new_concepts.gloss: the Ajivika school of Makkali (Gosala), with its atoms of five kinds and its fixed course of things, as rival schools report it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: ஆசீவகர்கள் (neelakesi 669) and the sarukkam's rubric ஆசீவக வாதச் சருக்கம்

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (ஆசீவக வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in earlier Neelakesi chapters, distinct from vaadham (alchemy)

source_issues: 665: line 4 (அந்திணையில் பேராற்றல்) is hard to divide; the sense of what the feet bestow is uncertain.
671: காழ்ப்பாடு is rare; it recurs at 694 and 699 as an Ajivika term, but its exact sense is not fixed by the text.
673: line 4 புகழ்பூ ரணனே is divided across பூ / ரணனே; it may name the speaker பூரணன் or call the Lord the Full One.
675: line 3 (புலமா கொலியொன் றொழிய முதற்காஞ் சலமாய்) is hard to divide; the quality assigned to earth is unclear.
677: line 2 குணமே யிலவாம் seems to deny the atoms qualities just after 676 assigns them; possibly corrupt.
681: ஒக்கலி and யோகலி, named as two gods, are otherwise unknown; the forms may be corrupt.
682: lines 3-4 are compressed and the turn of the argument is a reading.
